07 / ATP-PCr
SECTION 07 • METABOLIC PATHWAY 1

ATP-PCr / Phosphagen System

When ATP demand rises suddenly, the muscle needs a rapid response. The ATP-PCr system uses stored ATP + phosphocreatine (PCr) to regenerate ATP very quickly.

PCr + ADP + H⁺ ⇌ ATP + CREATINE
PART 1 • THE ROLE

Why does the muscle need the ATP-PCr system?

Exercise can increase ATP demand before the slower, sustained pathways can fully respond. The phosphagen system provides a rapid way to restore ATP.

01
ATP demand rises

When a maximal effort begins, muscle contraction starts immediately and ATP is used immediately.

Phosphocreatine rapidly regenerates ATP

PCr donates phosphate through the creatine kinase reaction, helping restore ATP very quickly.

PCr + ADP + H⁺ → ATP + creatine
STOP & THINK
Why is ATP-PCr especially useful at the beginning of a maximal effort?
PART 2 • THE CREATINE KINASE REACTION

Watch the phosphate move.

The key reaction is reversible. During a sudden increase in demand, the reaction can move toward ATP formation.

Rapid ATP resynthesis

Phosphocreatine donates its phosphate group to ADP through the creatine kinase reaction, rapidly regenerating ATP.

PART 3 • RATE VS CAPACITY

Very fast does not mean unlimited.

The ATP-PCr system is powerful because it can regenerate ATP rapidly, but its total phosphagen stores are limited.

03
Very rapid
RATE

The system responds quickly when ATP demand rises suddenly.

Small
CAPACITY

PCr availability limits how long it can dominate very high-power work.

THINK LIKE AN EXERCISE SCIENTIST
If ATP-PCr has the fastest rate, why can't it power a marathon mainly?
PART 4 • WHEN IS IT IMPORTANT?

Match the pathway to the task.

The ATP-PCr system becomes especially important when exercise requires very high power and rapid ATP supply.

04

Very high intensity

Maximal or near-maximal power demands make rapid ATP supply especially important.

Short duration

Seconds-long efforts are strongly supported by phosphagen stores.

Repeated efforts

Recovery between bouts matters because PCr must be resynthesised before the next high-power effort.

PART 5 • RECOVERY

What happens after the sprint?

The phosphagen story does not end when the athlete stops. PCr resynthesis progresses during recovery and is oxygen-dependent.

05
PREDICT
Why does the recovery interval matter before another maximal repetition?
APPLY IT • REPEATED SPRINTS

Can the athlete repeat the same power?

Now combine rate + capacity + recovery. A second maximal sprint starts from the physiological state created by the first sprint and the recovery interval.

Think about the athlete.

An athlete performs 6 × 5-second maximal sprints. The recovery interval is reduced from 3 minutes to 30 seconds.

DEMANDEach repetition creates a very high ATP demand.
CAPACITYPCr stores are limited and are partly depleted by each effort.
RECOVERYA shorter recovery gives less time for PCr resynthesis before the next repetition.
FINAL APPLICATION
In your own words: why might the athlete's later sprint output change when recovery is shortened?
Model answer: Shortening recovery reduces the time available for PCr resynthesis. The athlete may therefore begin the next sprint with less restored phosphagen availability, while other metabolic pathways still contribute to ATP resynthesis.
KEY TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
01 • Very rapid rate

ATP-PCr can regenerate ATP very rapidly when demand rises suddenly.

02 • Small capacity

Its phosphagen stores are limited, so it cannot provide the main sustained supply for long-duration exercise.

03 • High-power tasks

It is especially important during maximal or near-maximal, seconds-long efforts.

04 • Recovery matters

PCr resynthesis progresses during recovery and affects repeated high-power performance.
